subject: Hoffman et al. (2001)
object: Hoffman et al. (2001) reported a 6-year-old girl, one of a pair of twins, with isolated humoral immunodeficiency and a unique combination of dysmorphic features. These included microcephaly, micrognathia, sickle-shaped eyebrows, hypoplastic alae nasi, thenar hypoplasia, partial 4-5 toe syndactyly, recessed great toes, anterior anus, and hypoplastic labia minora. Radiographs showed triphalangeal thumbs and hypoplastic first metatarsals. She had postnatal growth retardation, and her development was substantially slower than her twin's.

subject: Hoffman et al. (2001)
object: Hoffman et al. (2001) reported that the girl had recurrent sinopulmonary infections and pneumococcal bacteremia. Laboratory evaluation showed hypogammaglobulinemia and absent B cells.

subject: Hoffman et al. (2001)
object: Hoffman et al. (2001) found a normal 46,XX karyotype in the patient.

subject: Hoffman et al. (2001)
object: Hoffman et al. (2001) searched the literature and the London Dysmorphology Database and found no recognizable syndrome matching the patient's combination of features. They suggested that she may represent a unique syndrome of unknown etiology.

subject: Edery et al. (2001)
object: Edery et al. (2001) described a three-generation family with B-cell immunodeficiency, distal limb abnormalities, and urogenital malformations.

subject: Edery et al. (2001)
object: Edery et al. (2001) suggested that the disorder in their three-generation family might be a novel autosomal dominant syndrome.

subject: Tischkowitz et al. (2004)
object: Tischkowitz et al. (2004) reported a second family with B-cell immunodeficiency, distal limb abnormalities, genitourinary malformations, and mild dysmorphic features, similar to a previously described family. They further delineated the phenotype in females and concluded that this was a true syndromic association.

subject: Tischkowitz et al. (2004)
object: Tischkowitz et al. (2004) observed autosomal dominant inheritance in the second reported family with BILU syndrome, as in the first family.

subject: Tischkowitz et al. (2004)
object: In affected individuals from both reported BILU families, Tischkowitz et al. (2004) found no mutation in the candidate gene HOXA13 by sequence analysis and no evidence of a microdeletion involving HOXA13 or the HOXA cluster as a whole.

subject: Hügle et al. (2011)
object: Hügle et al. (2011) reported a 7-year-old girl who had almost complete loss of B cells, facial dysmorphism, and malformations of the limbs and genitalia. Her mother had similar dysmorphic features and a milder form of the B-cell deficiency.

subject: Hügle et al. (2011)
object: Hügle et al. (2011) stated that Hoffman syndrome had originally been described as a sporadic case of humoral immunodeficiency, facial dysmorphism, and limb anomalies in a young girl. They believed that this case and their 2 patients had the same condition, and they reviewed the features of the 3 affected individuals.

subject: Kallish et al. (2011)
object: Kallish et al. (2011) reported a sporadic patient with ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome and an expanded phenotype. The patient had more significant hand and foot anomalies than previously reported in that syndrome. The authors noted that ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome is characterized by absent or hypoplastic eyelids, fusion defects of the mouth, abnormal ears, ambiguous genitalia, skin differences, and developmental delay.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) reported that sequencing of patients with B cell-restricted immunodeficiency revealed autosomal dominant mutations in TOP2B, which encodes a type II topoisomerase required to alleviate topological stress during DNA replication and gene transcription; they stated that their findings define a class of B-cell immunodeficiency and were the first description of a defined monogenic syndrome due to mutations in the essential gene TOP2B.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) noted that the syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency with facial dysmorphism and limb anomalies previously described in two unrelated families with autosomal dominant inheritance had subsequently been named Hoffman syndrome, with the genetic etiology unknown until their study.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) restudied two previously reported unrelated families with autosomal dominant syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency; the probands from each family presented with recurrent infections by polysaccharide-encapsulated bacteria, severe hypogammaglobulinemia, and absent CD19+ B cells, but had normal T-cell responses to mitogens. A third patient, initially reported as having an atypical presentation of Ablepharon-Macrostomia syndrome, was later found to have humoral immunodeficiency.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) tabulated immunologic laboratory values at diagnosis in 4 patients from 3 families (ages at presentation 7 years, 35 years, 6 years, and 5 years), showing absent or markedly reduced CD19+ B cells (0, 48, 0, and 0 cells/microliter), low total IgG (232, 631, 73, and 242 mg/dL), deficient or undetectable tetanus, diphtheria and H. influenzae B titers, normal CD3+, CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell counts, and normal mitogen stimulation; reduced CD16+ NK cell numbers were present in two patients.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) reported that Hoffman syndrome patients had no detectable B cells in the peripheral blood and did not form germinal centers, and did not generate protective serologic titers to immunization; however, detectable amounts of circulating immunoglobulins indicated that some B cells were present but below the clinical limits of detection, while numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes and T-cell mitogen stimulation were normal. No malignancy was observed in the patients or mice.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) performed whole genome sequencing of affected and unaffected persons in two unrelated families with autosomal dominant syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency, filtering for novel, dominantly inherited coding variants, and identified TOP2B as the only gene with nonsynonymous changes in only the affected patients in both families; in family 1 a heterozygous missense mutation c.1448C>T, p.S483L was found and in family 2 a de novo in-frame deletion c.1761_1763delAGA, p.EE587E. All mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and affected the TOPRIM (DNA gating) domain and highly conserved amino acids; TOP2B had a probability of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI) of 1.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) found, by independent reanalysis of clinical whole-exome sequencing in a third patient (family 3) initially reported as atypical Ablepharon-Macrostomia syndrome and later found to have humoral immunodeficiency, a heterozygous TOP2B variant c.1897G>A, p.G633S, which was absent from the 1000 Genomes Project, ESP6500SI, ExAC v0.3, and their in-house exome variant database, and was confirmed by Sanger sequencing; like the other mutations it affected the TOPRIM domain of TOP2B.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) showed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that chimeric yeast–human TOP2B constructs or yeast ScTOP2 vectors carrying the patient mutations S483L, EE587E, or G633S failed to complement the temperature-sensitive top2-4 allele at the nonpermissive temperature and did not allow recovery of top2-delta haploid spore clones, indicating that each patient mutation disrupts topoisomerase II function.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) demonstrated that yeast strains carrying one wild-type and one mutant copy of TOP2 (ScTOP2-EE587E or -S483L) grew more slowly than wild-type controls and that nuclear fractions from strains with the mutant alleles decatenated kinetoplast DNA less effectively than fractions containing a single wild-type copy, indicating that the disease-associated versions of TOP2 have a partial dominant negative phenotype.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) found that because Top2b-null mice do not survive the perinatal period, they bred Top2b-flox2 mice to cd19-cre and mb1-cre lines; Top2b-/-mb1-cre and Top2b-/-cd19-cre mice had fewer peripheral blood CD19+ B cells than wild-type littermates, with altered splenic follicle structure, reduced marginal zone and follicular B-cell zones, fewer PrePro B, Pre B and immature B cells in bone marrow, fewer splenic B cells at every developmental stage, reduced kappa-deleting recombination excision circles, and significantly reduced Pax5 with unchanged Rag1 expression.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) showed that Top2b-/-mb1-cre mice failed to produce ovalbumin-specific IgG after immunization and had impaired anti-Pneumovax-23 IgG3 and significantly reduced IgG2b responses, while PPV23-specific IgM and B-1 cells were unaffected; in vitro, LPS-stimulated Top2b-deficient B cells failed to proliferate, showed increased cell death by LDH release, and had less robust upregulation of MHC II, consistent with the failure to mount a vaccine response observed in patients.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) generated a constitutive knockin mouse carrying the murine equivalent of the patient TOP2B EE587E mutation; Top2bEE587E/EE587E homozygotes were not viable, as for Top2b-/- mice, whereas Top2b+/EE587E heterozygotes, mirroring the genotype of Hoffman syndrome patients, had reduced spleen-to-body ratio, reduced total serum IgG, significantly lower antigen-specific antibody titers after ovalbumin or Pneumovax-23 immunization, and reduced numbers of B cells at most stages of B-cell development in bone marrow and spleen, with reduced Pax5 and Foxo1 but unchanged Rag1 and E2A expression and normal Notch1 and Tcf1.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) compared Top2b+/EE587E knockin to Top2b+/- mice and found that, similar to patient proband A, Top2b+/EE587E mice had decreased peripheral blood B cells that were reduced even compared with Top2b+/- mice without an effect on peripheral blood T cells, and had reduced KRECs with unaffected TRECs, supporting a dominant negative rather than purely haploinsufficient mechanism; splenic B cells from Top2b+/EE587E mice also showed increased DNA strand breaks by comet assay while T cells were unaffected.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) found that B cells from Top2b+/EE587E mice stimulated in vitro with LPS with or without IL-4 secreted less total IgG, IgG3 and IgG2b than littermate controls, were reduced in number with greater LDH release, and more than 90% failed to advance beyond the first division after 5 days, whereas splenic T cells produced normal IL-2 in response to PMA and ionomycin and proliferated normally, consistent with the normal T-cell mitogen responses in patients.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) showed that wild-type mouse B cells have greater expression of Top2b mRNA and protein than T cells, consistent with previous reports in humans and mice, and proposed that the B cell-specific vulnerability reflects preferential reduction of long gene transcription when topoisomerases are absent, noting that murine B-cell transcription factor genes are longer (EBF 390 kb, Pax5 178 kb, Foxo1 85 kb) than T-cell (Tcf1 30 kb, Notch1 45 kb) or shared (Rag1 11 kb, E2A 24 kb) transcription factor genes; analysis of published Top2b ChIP-seq and END-seq data showed Top2b, but not Top2a, at the Pax5 promoter and intron 5 enhancer in murine primary B cells.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) noted that a brief clinical report had described a patient with progressive microcephaly, developmental delay, and hypotonia who had a TOP2B variant outside the TOPRIM domain (H58Y), but stated that no similarities to their patients were identified and that it was unclear whether that variant was causative.

subject: Broderick et al. (2019)
object: Broderick et al. (2019) concluded that in three families with Hoffman syndrome three heterozygous mutations affecting the TOPRIM (DNA gating) domain of TOP2B were identified and that yeast studies indicated these were partially dominant loss-of-function mutations, consistent with the nonviability of homozygous Top2bEE587E/EE587E mice; inheritance in the families was autosomal dominant.

subject: Papapietro et al. (2020)
object: Papapietro et al. (2020) studied 2 previously described unrelated families with autosomal dominant BILU syndrome (B-cell immunodeficiency, limb anomalies, and urogenital malformations), one from Cyprus (family A) and one from France (family B). The patients had absent or reduced B cells but normal T and myeloid cells.

subject: Papapietro et al. (2020)
object: Papapietro et al. (2020) performed multicolor flow cytometry on a bone marrow aspirate from BILU patient II:4 of family A and found complete absence of any CD19+ cells, including pro-B, pre-B, immature, and mature B cells, with normal T, NK, and myeloid lineages, indicating a block at the earliest stages of B-cell development after the common lymphoid progenitor stage. The block was described as leaky, since immunoglobulins and small numbers of B cells were found in peripheral blood of several patients.

subject: Papapietro et al. (2020)
object: In family A with BILU syndrome, Papapietro et al. (2020) used exome sequencing of 4 family members to identify a de novo heterozygous c.1453G>C mutation in the TOP2B gene, resulting in an ala485-to-pro (A485P) substitution. The mutation arose de novo in affected II:4 and was transmitted to her affected daughter. Sanger sequencing found the same mutation in patients of family B. The mutation was absent from more than 90,000 subjects in gnomAD. It affected an alanine conserved in eukaryotic and prokaryotic type II topoisomerases and was predicted to destabilize an alpha helix in the catalytic TOPRIM domain.

subject: Papapietro et al. (2020)
object: Papapietro et al. (2020) found reduced TOP2B protein in patient T cells, fibroblasts, and iPSCs. In TOP2B-knockout HEK293 cells, the A485P mutant showed a degradation product, suggesting it was less stable, but it still interacted with TOP2A. Purified recombinant A485P protein had more than 10-fold reduced DNA relaxation and decatenation activity. Patient T-cell blast lysates had reduced decatenation activity.

subject: Papapietro et al. (2020)
object: Papapietro et al. (2020) found that expressing TOP2B A485P in wildtype HEK293 cells, or co-expressing it with wildtype TOP2B in knockout cells, lowered decatenation activity compared with wildtype alone. They concluded that the mutant has a dominant-negative effect on wildtype TOP2B and TOP2A rather than causing haploinsufficiency. They noted that gnomAD contains 42 unaffected individuals with heterozygous loss-of-function TOP2B variants.

subject: Papapietro et al. (2020)
object: Papapietro et al. (2020) noted that other dominant TOP2B mutations in the TOPRIM domain cause Hoffman syndrome (B-cell deficiency, limb abnormalities, and facial dysmorphism). They concluded that BILU and Hoffman syndromes are manifestations of the same disease, TOP2B deficiency.

subject: Erdős et al. (2021)
object: Erdős et al. (2021) reported an inherited TOP2B mutation and suggested that it might confirm mutational hotspots in the TOPRIM domain of TOP2B.
